parts.text:
You design Thai language lesson scenarios. Given vocabulary words, create a vivid realistic scene where two Thai adult friends (not family members) naturally use these words. Characters A and B are friends or acquaintances — never parent/child, never siblings.

Vocabulary: รถเมล์=bus, ยาว=long, ครั้ง=time(s), occasion, คุ้ม=to be worthwhile, ทางเข้า=entrance, ควร=should, กังวล=to worry, รีบ=hurry, หวัง=hope, คู่=pair/couple, ชิ้น=piece/classifier, ไฟ=light/electricity, ต้องการ=want, need (formal), สามารถ=be able to (formal), เล่า=tell

Return ONLY valid JSON (no markdown):
{"scene":"2-sentence scene in English","characterA":"Thai man name and role","characterB":"Thai woman name and role","nameA_th":"A's name written in Thai script exactly as used in the Thai lines (e.g. สมชาย)","nameB_th":"B's name written in Thai script exactly as used in the Thai lines (e.g. นิดา)","opening":"Natural Thai greeting A says to B (must end ครับ). MUST warmly acknowledge the person — สวัสดีครับ is fine, or casual: วันนี้เป็นยังไงบ้างครับ, นานไม่ได้เจอกันเลยครับ, มาถึงแล้วเหรอครับ, เพิ่งมาถึงเหรอครับ, ว่างไหมครับ. BANNED: ไปไหนมาครับ (interrogation, not greeting). Make the other person feel welcomed.","opening_phonetic":"full romanisation of opening","opening_english":"English translation of opening (omit particle)","opening_prompt":"One sentence — ALWAYS use both character names (e.g. Somchai greets Nida and says it has been a long time). Never use vague he/she without naming the characters.","reply":"B greets A back and responds to what A said. ONE simple sentence only — must end with a single ค่ะ or คะ. Do NOT ask if something is wrong, if he has problems, or if he is troubled. Keep it warm and positive.","reply_phonetic":"full romanisation of reply","reply_english":"English translation of reply (omit particle)","reply_prompt":"Use B's name ONCE to open, then she/he only — NEVER repeat B's own name twice in one sentence. e.g. Nida greets Somchai back and says SHE is doing well (NOT: says Nida is doing well). No job titles.","closing":"Natural Thai parting A says to B to end the conversation (must end ครับ). Vary it — do not always use แล้วเจอกัน. Draw on: ไว้เจอกันใหม่ครับ, ดูแลตัวเองด้วยนะครับ, เดินทางปลอดภัยนะครับ, ขอให้เป็นวันที่ดีนะครับ, โชคดีนะครับ, แล้วคุยกันนะครับ, ฝันดีครับ. Must fit the time of day and the scene.","closing_phonetic":"full romanisation of closing","closing_english":"English translation of closing (omit particle)","closing_prompt":"One sentence naming A, e.g. Somchai says goodbye to Nida and tells her to take care.","closing_reply":"B's short parting back to A. ONE sentence, ends with ค่ะ. Should differ from A's wording — if A says see you again, B might wish him a safe trip.","closing_reply_phonetic":"full romanisation","closing_reply_english":"English translation (omit particle)","closing_reply_prompt":"One sentence naming B once, then she/he."}

CRITICAL: whatever Thai name/nickname you use in the opening and reply Thai fields, use the SAME name (romanized) in all English fields. No different English name for the same character.

Plan a language lesson conversation. LESSON THEME (broad — NOT a place every scene must happen in): Somchai tells Nida about his long bus ride to a new entrance, hoping it was worth the wait.
Characters: A = Somchai (a curious traveler) · B = Nida (a helpful local)
Group these target words into 2–7 MINI-SCENES (e.g. at the stall → paying → planning the trip). Each mini-scene gets a short purpose AND its OWN localPremise (where A and B are and what is happening in THIS scene), location and immediateGoal — a travel scene is about travel even if the lesson began at a food stall. Put each word where its NORMAL meaning fits best. Use every id exactly once. Prefer several coherent mini-scenes over one forced conversation.
CLUSTER BY MEANING: words of the same semantic domain belong in the SAME mini-scene — e.g. food words (meat, garlic, onion, lime, snacks) together; shopping/payment words (promotion, discount, card, credit card, transfer) together; home words (bedroom, kitchen, shower) together; big numbers (ten thousand, hundred thousand, million) together with prices; plans/schedule words (tired, probably, Thursday, wake up) together. Mini-scenes may have very different sizes (2 words or 10 words is fine) — never split a domain just to balance the sizes. The domain hint after each word is a suggestion.

You write Pimsleur-style Thai lessons. Write one exchange in an ongoing conversation.
SCENE: Somchai tells Nida about his long bus ride to a new entrance, hoping it was worth the wait.
A = Somchai, a curious traveler — MUST end every sentence with ครับ
B = Nida, a helpful local — MUST end every sentence with ค่ะ or คะ
RULES:
• A lines end ครับ. B lines end ค่ะ or คะ. NO EXCEPTIONS.
• CURRENT LEVEL: 10th Kyu · PREFERRED LENGTH: 3–5 Thai words · ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM: 7 Thai words (polite / question / sentence-final particles do not count). Prefer 3–5 — the shortest natural way to say it. Use 6–7 only when the idea or the lesson word cannot be said naturally more simply. Never exceed 7. A short natural reply ("yes", "okay", "really?") is fine — never pad a line. If a speaker needs to say more, split it into another turn.

DIALOGUE RULE: These are conversation pairs. Prompts describe what a character says in third person ("He says he likes...", "She asks if...") but the Thai sentence naturally uses first person ("ผม/ฉัน = I"). This is CORRECT and NEVER a mismatch.

PERSPECTIVE RULE (apply BEFORE comparing): the prompt narrates the SPEAKER in the third person; the Thai and English are the speaker's own words. Speaker A is a man: in A's prompt "he/him/his" = "I/me/my" (ผม) and "she/her" = "you" (คุณ, the listener). Speaker B is a woman: in B's prompt "she/her" = "I/me/my" (ฉัน) and "he/him" = "you" (คุณ). THAI LEXICAL FACTS: จ่าย (pay) is ordinary spoken Thai, never "too formal". 10,000 is หนึ่งหมื่น / หมื่น (สิบพัน is not idiomatic). พอดี means "just right / fits / exactly enough" (and พอดี… at the start = "it so happens"); English "just right" does NOT require เพิ่ง (เพิ่ง = "just" in time: has just happened). เจอ + a person = "meet / see"; เจอ + a thing = "find". พี่ can ADDRESS the listener ("you", someone a little older) or mean "older sibling" — judge which by context; either is correct Thai. หน่อย softens a request or asks for "a bit more" (ช่วยหน่อย, เร็วหน่อย); it does not attach to a descriptive adjective to mean "quite". A price of zero baht is only credible when something is free. A speaker variation that is merely stylistic is never an error.
